stages.name: Observe
stages.instruction: Sweep the three sliders and watch the inclinaison heatmap and compass arrow change. The magnetic pole (M) sits at geographic latitude $90^\circ - \alpha$. Advance when each slider has covered at least half its range.
stages.concept: Earth's field is modeled as a centered dipole tilted by angle $\alpha$ from the rotation axis. At magnetic latitude $\lambda_m$ the dip angle satisfies $\tan I = 2 \tan \lambda_m$. Declinaison $D$ is the horizontal deflection from geographic north.

stages.name: Experiment
stages.instruction: A target inclinaison $I^*$ is shown. The dashed curve (isocline) traces every position where the local inclinaison equals $I^*$. Move the compass onto that curve by tuning the sliders.
stages.concept: Every point on the isocline shares the same magnetic latitude $\lambda_m^* = \arctan(\tan I^* / 2)$. The curve is a small circle on the sphere centered at the magnetic pole M — many $(\lambda_g, \varphi, \alpha)$ triples land on it.

stages.name: Evaluate
stages.instruction: Heatmap and isocline are hidden. Only the target inclinaison $I^*$ is given. Compute a valid $(\lambda_g, \varphi, \alpha)$ on paper, then set the sliders. One submit per setup — a miss rotates you to the next scenario.
stages.concept: Invert the dipole formula. Fix $\varphi = 0$ (compass on the magnetic meridian) so $\lambda_m = \lambda_g + \alpha$. Then $\tan I^* = 2 \tan(\lambda_g + \alpha)$ solves as $\lambda_g = \arctan(\tan I^* / 2) - \alpha$.

labels.tip1: sweep each slider to at least half its range
labels.tip2: drag the compass onto the dashed isocline
labels.tip3: compute the parameters on paper, then set the sliders
labels.peek_tip_formula: fix phi=0 so lambda_m = lat + alpha; then lat = atan(tan(I*)/2) - alpha
labels.peek_tip_anchor: for I* = 60deg, tan(I*) = sqrt(3), so lambda_m ~ 40.9deg. subtract alpha to get lat.

1.1: Which slider changes the inclinaison the most? Try the latitude first.
1.2: Notice that longitude has little effect near the poles but a strong effect near the equator when alpha is large.
1.3: The dipole tilt alpha shifts the whole magnetic-latitude grid; sweep it and watch the heatmap slide.

2.1: The dashed curve is the isocline. Every point on it has the same local inclinaison.
2.2: Fix one slider (try phi = 0) and adjust the other two until the compass lands on the curve.
2.3: The isocline is a circle on the sphere centered at the magnetic pole M. Move around M at constant magnetic latitude.

3.1: Write the dipole formula: tan(I) = 2 tan(lambda_m). Solve for lambda_m first, then relate it to your sliders.
3.2: Pick phi = 0 and alpha = 11 (Earth's value). Then lambda_m = lat + alpha, so lat = atan(tan(I)/2) - 11.
3.3: Peek reveals the rearranged formula. Compute lat numerically for the given I*, then set the slider before you submit.
